title: Encryption & Hashing
objectives: Separate encoding, hashing and encryption by purpose
Pick the right tool for passwords, integrity and confidentiality

sections.markdown: The most common security confusion: treating **encoding, hashing and encryption** as interchangeable. They solve completely different problems.
Encoding is **Morse code** — anyone with the chart reads it back. Encryption is writing in a language only you and your friend share a key for.

## Hashing
- **One-way**: can't reverse it.
- **Deterministic**: same input → same hash; tiny change → totally different (avalanche).
- **Fixed length** regardless of input size.
Using fast hashes (MD5, SHA-1, plain SHA-256) for passwords — attackers brute-force billions/sec. Use slow, salted hashes: bcrypt, scrypt, argon2.
**Salt** = random per-password value added before hashing so identical passwords get different hashes and rainbow tables fail.
Hybrid/envelope encryption: use slow asymmetric crypto once to share a fast symmetric key, then AES for the data — exactly what TLS and KMS do.

flashcards.back: Encoding = reversible formatting (no key). Hashing = one-way digest. Encryption = reversible with a key.
So identical passwords hash differently, defeating rainbow tables and precomputation.
Symmetric (AES) = one shared key, fast. Asymmetric (RSA/ECC) = public/private pair, enables key exchange + signatures.

quiz.explain: Base64 just reformats bytes to ASCII — anyone can decode it. It is not security.
Slow, salted hashes resist brute force; fast hashes and encoding do not.
Hashing cannot be reversed to the original input; encryption can with a key.

challenges.text: Encode/decode a string to Base64 and URL-encoding; show round-trip equality.
Hash passwords with a salt using bcrypt; verify correct and reject wrong ones.
Encrypt and decrypt a file with AES-256-GCM, handling IV and auth tag.
Sign a message with RSA/ECDSA and verify with the public key.
